question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3}) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ and $v=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and $v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{2} & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=2{e}^{5x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is already in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=6$ and $Q(x)=2{e}^{5x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 6\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{6x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y) & ={e}^{6x}\cdot 2{e}^{5x} \\ {e}^{6x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{e}^{6x}\cdot y & =2{e}^{11x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{6x}) & =2{e}^{11x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{6x})\text{d}x & =\int 2{e}^{11x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{6x} & =\frac{2{e}^{11x}}{11}+C \\ y & =\frac{2{e}^{5x}}{11}+C{e}^{-6x}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y={x}^{2}{e}^{6x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-6$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}{e}^{6x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -6\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-6x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-6x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-6x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y) & ={e}^{-6x}\cdot {x}^{2}{e}^{6x} \\ {e}^{-6x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6{e}^{-6x}\cdot y & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-6x}) & ={x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-6x})\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-6x} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C \\ y & =\frac{{x}^{3}{e}^{6x}}{3}+C{e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y=9,\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below:

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{6}{x}$ and $Q(x)=9.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (6/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{6\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{6})} \\  & ={x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{6}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y) & ={x}^{6}\cdot 9 \\ {x}^{6}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{5}y & =9{x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{6})\,dx & =\int 9{x}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =\frac{9{x}^{7}}{7}+C \\ y & =\frac{9x}{7}+\frac{C}{{x}^{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}{{x}^{5}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{6}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}{{x}^{5}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (6/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{6\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{6}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y) & ={x}^{6}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}{{x}^{5}} \\ {x}^{6}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{5}y & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{6}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{6})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x,$ and $v=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{6} & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =x(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{3})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =x(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{3})+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{3}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{3}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}{9}\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}{{x}^{6}}}{9}-\frac{\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{{x}^{5}}}{3}+\frac{C}{{x}^{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation
$6\frac{dy}{dx} + y = 6x$.
Select the correct options below.
An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x) =$ {{field-1}}.

The general solution is given by $y(x) =$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First divide the equation by $6$ to write it in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}y=x
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{6}$ and $Q(x)=x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1/6\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x/6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x/6}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}y) & ={e}^{x/6}\cdot x \\ {e}^{x/6}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}{e}^{x/6}\cdot y & =x{e}^{x/6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/6}) & =x{e}^{x/6} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/6})\text{d}x & =\int x{e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts.

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}={e}^{x/6},$ and $v=6{e}^{x/6}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{e}^{x/6} & =\int x{e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =\frac{6}{6}\left(x(6{e}^{x/6})-\int 6{e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x\right) \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =6x{e}^{x/6}-6\int {e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =6x{e}^{x/6}-36{e}^{x/6}+C \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =6(x-6){e}^{x/6}+C \\ y & =6(x - 6) + Ce^{-x/6}.\end{aligned}
$$
